prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated free of Doppler, recoil and first-order light shifts, reaching fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye, and the reasons are the same experimental ones as in round 1, now tested against the chair's questions. The subject of the citation must be the lattice itself. The idea is that at the magic wavelength the differential light shift of the clock transition cancels, so that thousands of neutral atoms are confined in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated without Doppler and recoil shifts, while the statistical power of a many-atom ensemble is kept. Neither a comb (2005) nor single-ion control (2012) contains that idea, and it is what produced the step from the 1e-15 range to about 1e-18. The result is mature in the sense I care about: blackbody, higher-order lattice and density shifts are controlled by theory that agrees with measurement, and Sr and Yb clocks at RIKEN, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere agree at that level, including over intercontinental links. On the chair's timing question, I do not think the committee should wait for the SI redefinition. The prize would rest on demonstrated performance and its reproduction, and a redefinition would add to the case but is not required by it. On capability versus fundamental physics, I would be honest in the citation and lead with capability (a new regime of accuracy and stability), because the constants tests have so far given null results; the millimetre-scale redshift measurement is a real demonstration that nature is being probed with a new instrument, but it is secondary. On names, the record supports exactly two: Katori for the proposal and first Sr lattice clock, Ye for taking accuracy and stability to the frontier and the many-body Fermi-degenerate clock. A third seat would need a decisive contribution of a different kind, and no colleague has shown one.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes remains the strongest objection and is a judgement, not something I can prove away. A sceptic can read the lattice clock as the natural next step of precision spectroscopy, and Lindroth, Eriksson and Mehlig are right that it is a prize for an instrument more than for a surprise in nature. The credited pair also excludes Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Takamoto, Hinkley, Ludlow, Oates and the ion-clock lineage, and the historical question that Olsson and Mehlig raised, namely whether the proposal or the first operational Sr clock marks the original contribution, is not settled from the files in front of me and I am partly working from memory. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so part of the societal payoff is prospective.

responses.point: Ulf Danielsson moved B004 from eighth to first choice, argues that the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate invention from the comb, and asks that the citation name the lattice concept explicitly; he also says B004 is an instrument rather than a new phenomenon and warns against treating the count as the argument.
responses.response: I accept the warning and I have tried to rebuild the case without the count. Your distinction is the one I would defend to Eriksson: the comb counts optical cycles, while the magic-wavelength lattice is what allows many atoms to be held without perturbing the transition, and the two-order improvement over caesium comes from that, not from the comb. I have therefore written the citation around the lattice, the cancellation of the light shift, and the absence of Doppler and recoil shifts. On instrument versus phenomenon I concede the point and do not think the committee should pretend otherwise. The Nobel tradition in physics has often rewarded instruments that opened a new measurement regime, and here the evidence is experimental and reproduced, but I would not lean on the constants tests, which so far are null results.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson prefers B010 as a discovery of new quantum states of matter, argues that opening support is not merit and that a clock prize extends a lineage recognised in 2005 and 2012, but says he would not stand in the way if atomic-physics colleagues judge B004 sufficiently distinct, and asks that B010 be considered for a following year.
responses.response: You asked atomic-physics colleagues to state the distinction in terms you can evaluate, so here it is as plainly as I can. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a ruler for optical frequencies. The 2012 prize recognised control of single trapped quantum systems, with the Al+ ion clock as one application. Lattice clocks use neither idea for their defining step. They solve a different problem, which is how to hold a large ensemble of neutral atoms with Doppler, recoil and light shifts simultaneously removed, and the solution is a specific wavelength condition set by the dynamic polarizabilities of the two clock states. That is a separate invention with a separate quantitative outcome. I share your view that opening support is not merit and I do not claim B004 is a discovery of a new phase; I claim it is the best-verified new measurement capability on the list. I fully agree that B010 is a strong theory-then-experiment case and I have moved it into my alternatives for that reason. My reservations remain device variability, the open pairing mechanism, and Cao's omission, which I think should wait for a later year.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth argues that the magic-wavelength condition is genuinely atomic-structure physics, depending on dynamic polarizabilities and higher-order light shifts, and asks that the citation name the lattice and magic-wavelength concept so that it is not read as a general clock prize.
responses.response: I agree and have adopted that wording. Your point about dynamic polarizabilities also sharpens my own experimental argument: the claim of 1e-18 is credible only because the higher-order light shifts and the blackbody shift are understood quantitatively, and that understanding is atomic-structure physics, not just engineering. Where I still differ slightly is on how much to say about nature being tested. The citation should lead with the lattice and the accuracy and mention redshift or constants only as consequences, because the constants limits are null and a reader at the Academy should not be able to say we oversold them.

responses.point: Eva Olsson asks that the historical record be checked, namely whether Katori's proposal (around 2001-2003) or the first operational strontium lattice clock marks the original contribution, and cautions that B034 has a Blais-versus-Girvin attribution problem and a 2025 timing problem.
responses.response: On B034 I now agree with you and have moved it out of my alternatives, since a four-name story forced into three is the weakest form of credit and the 2025 prize has just recognised superconducting circuits. On the historical point, I think the answer is that both are Katori's. The proposal of trapping neutral atoms in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength came from his group, and the first operational Sr lattice clock was also from his group, at about the same time as the SYRTE group's Sr work. The citation wording 'invention and realisation' covers that without choosing between them. I cannot fully settle the contemporaneous contributions of Lemonde's group from memory, and I would ask that the committee secretariat check the dated record before the citation is finalised, but I would not let that change the two-name conclusion, because priority for the lattice concept itself is not in doubt.

responses.point: Bernhard Mehlig supports B004 because the precision rests on a mechanism one can write down and analyse, but notes that it is largely a refinement of precision spectroscopy and that a two-name prize sets a hard boundary against Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates.
responses.response: I agree that the mechanism is what carries the case and not the number. On the boundary, the question I put to myself is whether any further person made a decisive contribution of a different kind to the invention. Lemonde and Takamoto were part of the early demonstrations and Ludlow and Oates produced important records, but these are, in my reading, parallel realisations or later improvements of a concept already stated and demonstrated, which is the kind of contribution that historically falls outside a three-person limit. Ye's contribution is of a different kind because of the many-body clock and the sustained systematics programme that set the field's benchmark. I would not claim this is beyond argument, and I accept that the hard boundary is real, but I think two names is the more faithful reading of the record than any three-name set I can construct.

responses.point: Mark Pearce, as chair, raises whether a second part (B032 or B036) should be added or whether a single two-person prize is cleaner, and observes that B004 and B036 would be a poor pairing in the same year.
responses.response: I agree that a second part is not worth adding. B036 shares laser-cooling and atom-optics heritage with B004 and would blur the credit I value in the single-topic prize. B032 is a real observational window, but I accept your own maturity reservation, that source associations are still at modest significance, and its credited set is a harder attribution problem than the clock pair. A single-part prize gives a clean citation and the strongest verification, and I would not dilute it to reach an extra count.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will finally judge the lattice clock distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I think it is, but I recognise this is a judgement that colleagues outside atomic physics cannot check independently.

The exact dated priority between Katori's proposal, the first Sr lattice clock, and the contemporaneous SYRTE work, which I am partly recalling from memory and which the secretariat should verify before a citation is fixed.
Whether limiting credit to two names omits a decisive contribution that I am not weighing correctly, for example by Lemonde or Takamoto.
Whether the SI second will be redefined soon enough to change how the citation reads, and whether the committee prefers to wait.
statement.conflict_note: No personal conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. I have an adjacency to the field of B004, B036 and B013 through atomic physics and rare-earth quantum-memory work, with no direct collaboration with any named candidate that I know of. I serve on the management team of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, which is Chalmers-led and overlaps with superconducting-qubit work (B034, B043), and I hold a company role at Deep Light Vision AB; neither bears on B004, and since I no longer list B034 among my alternatives the first overlap is now only a disclosure.
